passage: In the school gym in Valencia, the basketball coach pinned up the shooting stats. Next to Alejandro's name: "Missed 40%." He read it and felt his chest drop. That evening he told Freya he was thinking of quitting the team. "Forty percent failure, Freya. That's almost half." Freya pulled up her own sheet on her phone. On the girls' team sheet, the coach had written each player's number the other way round: "Scored 60%." "Your number's the same as mine," she said. "I felt great about mine." Alejandro stared at the two sheets. "Sixty percent sounds... good, actually." He stopped talking about quitting.

qa.q: What did the sheet say next to Alejandro's name?
qa.a: The sheet said "Missed 40%."

qa.q: Why did Alejandro think of quitting the team?
qa.a: Seeing his result written as a 40 percent failure made it feel like almost half was bad, which dragged his mood down and nearly his choice with it.

qa.q: What habit could help Alejandro when he sees a percentage like this?
qa.a: He could rewrite it both ways, missed and scored, before reacting, so the wording doesn't make his decisions for him.

qa.q: How might Freya feel about having the same number and feeling great?
qa.a: Freya may be amused and a little surprised that the same result could make one friend proud and the other ready to quit.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy ready to quit over a result worded as 40 percent missed, until the same figure framed as 60 percent scored changes his mood.

passage: At the coaching institute, the mock-test results appeared on the corridor screen: "Dhruv: 40% incorrect." Dhruv went pale and walked straight past the canteen. In the counselling room, Sarita ma'am found him staring at the floor. "I'm failing, ma'am. Forty percent wrong." She turned her laptop toward him. "Look at your printed report card instead." It said: "Accuracy 60%. Batch average 52%." Dhruv read it twice. "That's the same test?" "Same test, same you." "Then why does the screen say it like that?" Sarita ma'am sighed. "Someone chose that wording. Your reaction came from the words, not from the score." Dhruv looked a little less pale.

qa.q: What was the batch average on the printed report card?
qa.a: The batch average was 52%.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv go pale and skip the canteen?
qa.a: Dhruv felt ashamed and worried because the screen framed his result as 40% incorrect, so it felt like failing. That wording, not the score itself, sank his mood.

qa.q: What could the institute change about how results are shown?
qa.a: It could show accuracy and the batch average together, or both correct and incorrect, so students don't react to one gloomy word.

qa.q: How might Sarita ma'am feel about the corridor screen?
qa.a: Sarita ma'am seems frustrated with the wording, since it made a student feel he was failing when his score was above average.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy crushed by a result worded as 40 percent incorrect until he sees the same score framed as 60 percent accuracy.

passage: Last year, the career counsellor at school ran our marks through a chart and said, "Vaibhav, there's a forty percent chance you won't make the cut-off for the design college." I went back and asked the counsellor to say it the other way. Sixty percent. It felt like a different future. I applied. I got in, but even if I hadn't, at least the choice would have been mine, not the sentence's.

In Sahil's kasba school near Jalgaon, the headmaster read out the mock-test results by the Class 10 notice board.

"Sahil. Forty percent of questions wrong in science."

Sahil's stomach dropped. Forty percent wrong. He walked home past the cotton gin feeling like a failure. That night he told his sister Swati, "I'm dropping science. I'll take arts. I'm clearly not good enough."

Swati looked at the marksheet. "Sahil, this says sixty percent right."

"It's the same thing."

"Then why does it feel like a failure one way and okay the other?"

He looked at the paper. Sixty percent right. That didn't sound so bad. Last term, he'd got fifty.

"You were about to change your whole stream because of one sentence," Swati said.

He folded the marksheet into his science book. His mood lifted, just a bit. But he was surprised at how close he'd come.

qa.q: What percentage did the headmaster say Sahil got wrong?
qa.a: Forty percent of questions wrong in science.

qa.q: Why did Sahil decide to drop science after the announcement?
qa.a: Sahil felt like a failure and ashamed because "forty percent wrong" sounded so bad, even though it also meant sixty percent right.

qa.q: What did Swati do that helped Sahil rethink?
qa.a: Swati read the same result as sixty percent right and compared it with last term, which showed Sahil was actually improving.

qa.q: What would have changed if the headmaster had said sixty percent right?
qa.a: Sahil might have felt okay or even pleased, and wouldn't have thought of changing streams.

grounding: A teenager in a small town nearly drops science after hearing "forty percent wrong", until the same result is framed as sixty percent right.

passage:
At basketball practice in Guadalajara, the coach read out shooting stats. "Javier. Missed four of ten free throws."

Javier's face burned. He'd thought he was getting better. On the bus home, he texted his friend Ada: "I'm quitting the team. I'm terrible."

Ada called him right away. "What did you actually shoot?"

"Four misses out of ten."

"So six in."

"...Yes."

"Last month you said three in."

He paused. Six out of ten. Up from three. He hadn't even thought of it that way.

"Why does 'missed four' sound so bad?" he asked.

"Because 'missed' is a scary word," Ada said. "The numbers are the same."

Javier looked out of the bus window. Two minutes ago he'd been ready to quit. Now he was thinking about extra practice on Saturday.

qa.q: How many free throws did the coach say Javier missed?
qa.a: Missed four of ten free throws.

qa.q: Why did Javier want to quit the team?
qa.a: Javier felt embarrassed and terrible because "missed four" made his shooting sound like failure.

qa.q: How did Ada help Javier see the facts differently?
qa.a: Ada turned "missed four" into "six in" and compared it with last month's three, showing real improvement.

qa.q: How might the coach's wording have affected other players?
qa.a: Other players may also have felt discouraged hearing their misses, even if they were improving.

grounding: A teenager abroad nearly quits a team after hearing "missed four of ten", until the same result is framed as six made.
